idiom_name: serde tagged enum: #[serde(tag = "type")] (internally tagged), adjacently tagged, or externally tagged
implementation_notes: Rust's sum type replaces the subclass registry: model the message as an enum and let serde place the tag - internally tagged (#[serde(tag = "type")]) puts the discriminator beside the variant fields, the adjacent form (tag plus content) keeps it separate so tuple variants fit, and the default external form wraps the payload in the variant name. The derived Deserialize impl is the dispatcher, rename/rename_all is the wire vocabulary, and #[serde(other)] on a unit variant turns unrecognized tags into a catch-all instead of an error. Reach for a hand-written registry (a map from tag to a deserializer function, or deserialize to serde_json::Value first) only when the variant set is genuinely open and cannot be enumerated in the binary.
code_sketch:
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "kebab-case")]
enum Event {
    OrderCreated { id: String, total: u64 },
    OrderCancelled { id: String, reason: String },
    #[serde(other)]
    Unknown,                       // catches tags this binary does not know
}
pitfalls: The internally tagged form cannot represent tuple variants - #[serde(tag = ...)] on an enum with one is a compile-time error - and newtype variants holding non-map types fail at runtime with an invalid-type error, so use the adjacent form when payloads are not objects.
Untagged enums try variants in order and report only the last error, so a shape matching two variants binds the first: that is inference, not the pattern.
#[serde(other)] makes unknown tags silent successes; route the catch-all variant somewhere (dead-letter, warning, metric) or a renamed tag disappears without a trace.
